segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: And my wife's driving me nuts. My wife is--

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: Getting mad, because he's sticking his head in the sand.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Sticking my head in the sand. But like I said, I try to not think in that way. But like I said, we are-- we are totally different persons.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: These are the conversations the girls were overhearing.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel and Jenni have been married 17 years. Happily. They met salsa dancing. He stepped on her foot. She said, you owe me an ice cream. They spent the night talking at Denny's. These days, they still salsa dance in the living room, and corner off weekend mornings just for talking. When I asked Fidel to describe who's who in the relationship, this is how he frames the answer.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I always tell her it's is the positive and the negative. It's the positive and the negative.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Because you're an electrician, it's funny that you're saying positive and negative, because that's--

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Yeah. It's like how the battery works, how the car works. Because I always think positive. But she always looks at reality. She's the one saving money. She's the one making sure everything in the house works. All the paperwork is right, make sure the girls got the ride to school.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni posts to-do lists around the house. He executes, crossing each item off as he goes along. That's how they both like it.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: He is the fun dad. He does all the fun things. He takes the kids out for ice cream, and he spoils them. And if it's the disciplinarian, that's me.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: He is not the disciplinarian at all.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel's style is more to try and tease the girls into listening to him. For instance, McKenzie likes to wear short shorts. So one day Fidel said, hey, if you're going out like that, I'll do it too. He grabbed scissors, and cut off the bottom of his T-shirt, and made it into a crop top. Then, he reached for his shorts.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I cut them, and I stuck it up all the way up, like I stuck it up all the way up. Like hey, you're gonna to go to the street like that? Hey, let me go too. We can go together.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Was she embarrassed? What'd she say?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: She said, I'm not going to go with you like that.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: My dad is like-- he's very obnoxious.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Isabella is always, you're annoying me. Even Jennifer said, stop being annoying. And even McKenzie says, stop annoying. It's love. I don't know if it's annoying to them, but it's love.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: In January, on the first day of President Trump's second term, he declared a border emergency, moved to end birthright citizenship, and suspended refugee admissions. Within weeks, the TV was full of ads, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem telling immigrants--

segments.speaker: Kristi Noem
segments.text: Leave now. If you don't, we will find you, and we will deport you. You will never return.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni had tried to find out everything about the Trump administration's plans. She'd read about Project 2025, and worried that if Fidel got picked up, he'd get stuck in a detention center, and it would ruin their lives. She'd heard horror stories, people being treated cruelly, getting abused. She couldn't stop picturing Fidel in there, in a cell with nowhere to sleep, no way to call. What if he came out a completely different person than he went in? She didn't want that for her sweet goofball of a husband. And would they have to spend their life savings to get him out? One couple they were friends with, the husband had gotten picked up.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: They are over $50,000 in debt to attorneys. So you have destroyed, absolutely destroyed, this couple's life.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: But Fidel told her he was willing to take the risk. He wanted to stay.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: And I said, so what do you want to do if you get picked up? Tell me what that looks like. So if we're just going to take our chances and we're going to stay, what happens if you get picked up? During that conversation, he said, I don't want you to spend any money to get me out, if he were to get picked up for anything.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: And I told him that he needed to tell his children that. Because if something were to happen, they would never forgive me. They would never forgive me for leaving him in there. Even if it was a decision that he and I made together, they would never forgive me. Because I'm the fixer for all these kind of things.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel felt that unless ICE was here-here, like in their small suburban town an hour outside of Raleigh, North Carolina, there really wasn't much to worry about. He figured the odds were with him. When they were having these conversations last winter, ICE had arrested less than half of 1% of the 14 million undocumented people in the country.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Besides, Trump was still saying that he was going after criminals, and Fidel didn't see himself as a criminal. He was a tax-paying dad, a successful electrician helping build public schools in the area. If Fidel got detained and deported, it'd be disastrous, but it was just so unlikely.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni wasn't going to wait around for Fidel to agree with her to make a plan. She started prepping on her own, holed herself away in her home office, and got to work putting together these massive purple binders of pay stubs, receipts, paperwork.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: His birth certificate, a copy of all of his passports and identification, copies of our tax returns.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Hundreds of documents, in the case of his arrest or detainment, that she could use to prove that Fidel had been here, working, not committing crimes, for the past 30 years. She labeled the binders "in case of emergency." Fidel found it all a little bit--

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Annoying. Like annoying, like she wanted me to go, like she wanted me to go.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Did it hurt your feelings, this idea that she might want you to go?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I guess, yes. Just like, why do you want me to go? It's like, my life is in here. That is-- it hurts.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Did you ever tell her that it hurt your feelings?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: No, I think it's like a-- like a proud, how you say? Proud? Proud thing. I'm not going to tell you what hurts.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: McKenzie and Bella could understand both parents arguments over whether he should go. But it was easier to side with their dad. He was saying there was nothing to worry about, everything was fine, and things could stay the same.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Me and Bella both swayed to the side of keeping my dad in the United States.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: We kind of just didn't want him to go, so we kind of just-- I don't know if we avoided it, more like we just didn't really think about it, I guess.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: It'd be a shadow, and I definitely feel like it would come out, though, when we were at home, and if we weren't doing anything. If we were being a family, it would be like, oh, this might come to an end.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They'd been sitting with some version of this dread for over five years. They first learned that their dad might have to move to Mexico back in 2020, when Donald Trump was running for a second term. They were in fifth and seventh grade, and their mom, Jenni, was scared of what Trump would do with immigration in a second term and felt like she had to prepare the girls, who at that time had no idea at all that their dad was undocumented, or that he might have to leave. Of course, this was life-altering news.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I was crying, I know that.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Were you crying too?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Yeah, definitely.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I distinctly remember trying to hide the fact that I was crying by putting my hand right here, and then I would lay down on the desk, and my arm like that. Like, I did not want to be crying. So yeah, the thing is, I don't like the feeling of it on my face, really. So when I try to cry, I try to get it before it gets like down to here area. So--

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Their parents asked them not to tell anyone, which made this big news feel even heavier. Suddenly they felt different from the other kids at school.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Things started to also just make more sense. Because also people describe, when you're married, the man's supposed to drive. And then I'm like, oh, but my dad doesn't drive. And then I was like, oh, that's probably why. Because he doesn't have a license.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel does drive. But when the family's together, Jenni's the one who drives.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I started understanding why we didn't travel as much. I heard my friends all the time saying they traveled to Canada, or Europe, or whatever. I don't know what a five-year-old is doing in Europe, but whatever. But it was like I could hear them traveling, and I was like, why don't we ever travel? And so I kind of started understanding why.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: With this new understanding came fear. McKenzie started having nightmares about ICE.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: They come and break into the house, almost like a movie. And then we know that they're coming, but we're all hiding in the house behind the TV. And then they find my dad, and I'm standing, hiding away. But I still see him, and they're just taking him away.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: That was in seventh grade. She's older now, but the nightmares returned when Trump took office again and she started overhearing her parents arguing. The situation was back.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Do you guys ever talk about it amongst yourselves?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I actually don't think we've talked about it.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Yeah, no, we don't really talk about it.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I think that we both do the same thing, where--

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: We try to avoid it in conversation.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I don't think we've ever brought it up willingly just to talk. Because it's just like, we're going to sit there and be sad.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Instead, they dealt with the tension in the house by distracting themselves.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I think-- there was at one point, McKenzie had a running phase, where she ran every night.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Oh, yeah, I ran every night, during the winter time. Because Trump had just won, and then all these things were just running in my head.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: And she doesn't like running in the light, because she doesn't like people looking at her while she runs.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: So when it'd get dark, she would run, and I would ride my bike next to her. Because I cannot run for anything, like it's so bad. But yeah.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Would you guys talk too?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I think when I would be walking, we would talk, but it would be about school drama.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They'd run and bike for as long as they could, until it was too late to be out, and only then would they go home, traipse past their parents watching the evening news, and go upstairs.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: It's not like I don't care about what's going on. It's more like it's just sad. And it's like, well, if you're going to be sad forever, or you're going to block it out, and just move on or something.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: But the Trump administration did not want anyone to block out what they were doing. They wanted their immigration policies splashed across headlines and social media. They wanted them embedded in the nation's psyche, especially in families like this one. In March, the headlines were, Kilmar Abrego Garcia was mistakenly deported from Maryland to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador, along with 260 other people. The Trump administration added a self-deport button to the Customs and Border Protection app.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Meanwhile, McKenzie was working weekends at Jersey Mike's. Bella was on the wrestling team. She and Fidel practiced grappling in the living room. He drove the girls to soccer games most weekends, cheering them on from the sidelines.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni taped little cards all over the front door on red construction paper, what to do if ICE comes knocking. Bella's 15th birthday was coming up, her quinceañera year, a big deal. Fidel and Jenni kept asking her about plans and ideas for the party, but she just kept pushing it off. At one point her parents even asked her, do you want a quince, or a car instead? Quince, she said.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I wanted one. But then I was like-- I was thinking about it, and I was like, what if he's not actually there for it? The dad is a big part of a quince. So I was like, what if he's not even there to celebrate it with me? Do I really want that? And I was like, I don't want a quince without him. So I didn't want to go through all the trouble of planning it, and then him not being there. So I was like, oh, I don't want to do this anymore. So--

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: She called it off.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I was not happy with that. It's like, I just want to do the party. I just want to see Isabella happy. But it is what it is. We need to plan it and everything, and have that stress. And for some reason it would happen and oh, your dad is not going to be there in the party. I think that would be a pretty bad thing to happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Valerie Kipnis. Coming up, the pressure on the family increases, and the kids overhear something they haven't heard before. That's in a minute on Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. Today's program, Under One Roof, stories of families going through experiences, where different family members see things very differently from each other. We're in the middle of Valerie Kipnis's story about the Rivera family trying to figure out if they should self-deport. We pick up in the spring.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The stalemate between Jenni and Fidel was getting worse. Every day, Jenni went online, trying to think through a possible move. She scrolled through houses in Mexico, tried to find towns they could afford with expat communities. She looked up English language schools for the girls, who don't speak Spanish. She showed all this to Fidel, and he went along with it, begrudgingly. He didn't think it was necessary.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And all these months of pressure, of arguing, culminated in this one fight, when Jenni and Fidel found themselves standing across from each other in the living room, yelling. No one can remember what started the fight. What they do remember is the yelling.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I think the kids are upstairs, and they hear that stuff.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: How do you know?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I'm pretty sure they hear. We yelling pretty loud stuff. We're yelling pretty loud each other. It's like-- I'm thinking, in the top of my head, it's like, are you crazy? It's not going to happen. We yell at each other.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Was that unusual for you?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Yes, that is unusual. Because, like I said, 17 years, we never yell on each other, right? That is when my head start thinking, she's over stressed. And it's like this is when-- now is when my head start to kick in, it's like, I need to do something, I need to-- I need to start thinking.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The truth was, Fidel's resolve was starting to unravel. He had always believed that until job sites near him got raided, he was OK. There was nothing to worry about. But by the spring, ICE arrests in North Carolina had more than doubled since the same time last year. He started counting heads at work. Was anyone missing? He started getting nervous whenever he was driving, or when he saw a cop.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: In May, the Trump administration created Project Homecoming, offering people $1,000 and a free plane ticket to leave the country. They regularly posted triumphant videos on social media of agents with gaiters and guns blasting doors, raiding people's homes and workplaces, of people in shackles being led onto planes, often to the tune of trolling music.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: [POLICE CHATTER]

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: Come to the front door.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel watched those videos and others that were going viral, and they had the effect on him that the Trump administration probably wanted. They scared him.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I think I saw it on the TV, when the kids separated with the parents, that videos, where they grabbed the mom, and separate the mom, and the kids stay crying all day, the mom never coming back, and the kids thinking, what am I going to do? It's like, I don't want that feeling for my kids. I don't want to give them that feeling.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: One day, McKenzie saw reports on social media that ICE was in their area. She texted her parents. Fidel texted her back a goofy face emoji and, "don't worry about it." But it bothered him that she was thinking about this stuff.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I called him in June to check in. His friend's brother, who worked nearby, his job site had just been raided. And Fidel was preoccupied with two bills in front of the North Carolina legislature that would force state agencies like Highway Patrol to cooperate with ICE.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Almost all last year, when Jennifer tell me, it's like, hey, when we start to make a plan, it's like, oh, I don't think it's nothing going to happen. But now, it's-- especially with these two bills. It's like, oh, I think it's-- I think my wife is right.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Wow, Fidel, last time that you and I spoke, you were kind of like, I don't know, she's a bit dramatic, I don't know if I need to do this.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It's a big change.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Yes, it's-- every day I was like a little bit processing. It's like I need to start thinking and I need to change my switch.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The last straw for Fidel was Alligator Alcatraz.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I'm not-- I'm not going to be in one of that places. That is my switch. When Jennifer told me five months ago, hey, they're going to build detention centers. And even I told her, it's like, are you crazy? They're not going to build. And three months later, it's like, we got the first one. And I'm pretty sure maybe it's going to be more.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: After all those months, all those conversations, Fidel finally agreed that he needed to leave, maybe with the family, but probably alone. So in June, he sat Jenni down.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: The Saturdays or Sundays, we sit on the couch in the mornings. And I-- I told her, it's like, OK, fine, I'm going, I gotta go. Yeah. It's like, are you sure? And I say, yes. Like, the face changes right away.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Like she was relieved?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Like a relief on her face, like, I think finally he understands. Like, finally. Yeah, but yeah. It's-- it's good, it's fine.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: This is what Jenni had been asking for all along. She's had such a hard time watching the Trump administration's war against immigrants escalate.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: But I've already been living in that fear and panic for 16 years, and I can't take any more. And maybe if I was a different person, I could wait it out. But I'm not. I am who I am.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Something I think a lot is, people who do support Trump, if they were to think about this, they would feel like this is the point, is for people to be scared, is for people to leave, to self-deport, right? And it feels like-- is there a part of you that feels like this is admitting, like raising the white flag, and being like, you won? Or no?

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: Yeah. Feels like you're giving up. It absolutely does. But if you'd been living in the purgatory that we've been in for all of these years, and you weren't able to make any plans for your future, for your kids' future, for your life, at some point, everybody is going to raise that white flag. And so I am. I just can't do it anymore.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Meanwhile, Fidel has spent decades feeling like even though he entered the country illegally, he was here now, and he'd do things by the book, work hard at his job, pay into Social Security he'll never get back, support his kid's soccer team and Girl Scout troops, hoping that the people of America would see what he and so many other people were doing, that they were already contributing to this country, and embrace them, and make them full citizens. But now, he realized that deal was never going to come. In fact, a lot of people didn't even want him here.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He couldn't stop thinking about how hard he'd worked to make it in this country, picking oranges and tobacco. He'd started as a sweeper at his electrical company, worked his way up for years.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I think that is one of the reasons I feel like I'm angry, is because you are at the top of your career.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel's at the peak of his career, running projects and crews.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Like, I worked so hard. I worked so hard. Work, start from the bottom, and go all the way up. And now, I'm going to start again. But now, the difference is I'm 50 years old. I'm not 30 years old. My legs is not going to be the same. And my hands is not going to be the same.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Next, Fidel and Jenni told the girls their dad would leave after Christmas, and the girls didn't really take it seriously. They'd been talking about Fidel leaving for months. This just felt like another update, so far away. For months, Jenni had been gaming out their Mexico options, and they weren't great. There was the money. She had just a few more years, five years before she could get her full pension. If she moved away now, they could live comfortably in Mexico, but probably never could come back to live in the US again. They couldn't afford it. So she decided she probably wouldn't move. It wasn't worth it.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: As for the girls, she couldn't find them a public school with a good English-speaking program. But she wanted this to be a family decision. So Jenni called the girls into the living room for a family meeting.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: We were all sitting downstairs, over there on the couches. I'm sitting in the middle, and my mom's over there on that couch by herself, and my dad's sitting next to me.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: And I think I'm on the floor.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Yeah, I think you're on the floor.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni held up her iPad. On it was the listing for a house in Mexico. She was like, check out this house I found, maybe we could all move down to Mexico together. Would you want to live there, go to school there? McKenzie, the older sister, was the first to respond.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I think I said no to begin with. I was like, I don't want that. Didn't we have a whole thing, Bella?

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: She was so adamant that she did not want to move.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Oh, yeah. It was bad. I remember not wanting to leave the country at all. Because I mean, this is my only place that I've been-- born here, raised, North Carolina.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: So it was like, you're going to make me leave, when I've dedicated my work and my school to North Carolina, and to the United States? That didn't make any sense. I said, I don't want to leave. This makes-- I was like, it doesn't make any sense for me to want to go, because I'm-- this is my senior year. This is my last year at the school. You're not giving me enough time. And then my mom got mad, and she responded at me, your dad is dealing with this. It's causing me stress, it's causing the family stress. It's, like, intense around here because of what's going on.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: And then Bella didn't say anything. I don't think my dad really said anything. I think me and my mom were just rapid firing against each other. And then Bella kind of came and defended me, I guess. She was like, I see why McKenzie doesn't want to go, and you need to just let her be for a little bit. And my mom was saying, oh, you need to come back here. We still need to talk. And then my dad probably said the same thing, and I was like, I don't really have anything to say. I don't want to go, and I don't want to hear about all your plans about moving.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I said no to everything in general, like moving, thinking about moving, thinking about my dad leaving, thinking about the house, thinking about, I don't know, everything. I was saying, I don't want anything to happen. I just want it to stay how it is.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I mean, I was chill with whatever. Honestly, that's what I said. I was like, I don't really care what happens. I do care, I do. But you can literally take me out of the country. I could care less where I go. Like, I'll stay here, I'll leave. I'll do online school. I don't know, I'll just-- I didn't really care for it. I do care. Stop looking at me like that.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Why are you looking at her like that?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: I'm not looking at her like anything. She just sounds weird.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I was going to do whatever my mom thought was best. Leaving or staying, that's what I was going to do. And I get why McKenzie didn't want to leave either. I think my mom was really upset about the fact that she didn't want to leave, but I get why she didn't. Because she is literally like one year away from 18. And you're not going to really make any new friends at a new school for senior year.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Jenni had always thought that this was where the girls would land. The girls felt like Jenni was asking a question she already had the answer to. Fidel sat there quietly during this whole conversation, not saying much at all.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Did you secretly wish that everyone said, OK, let's all go? Or no?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Honestly, yeah, I'd say, yeah, everybody, let's go. If McKenzie said, yeah, we can go. And Bella said, yeah, we can go. And Jennifer said, yeah, we can go. It's like, then I had, sure, let's go. But that's like a movie stuff. In the real life, it's not gonna-- it's not gonna happen.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel's sister went to see the house in Mexico. It's four bedrooms with a small pool, not far from the beach. She called him afterwards and told him it was really nice, a smart investment. When Fidel heard, his heart dropped. There was no backing out now. He'd have to be there to sign the documents in September, in three weeks. He was really leaving. Jenni was out of town, and asked Fidel to be the one to tell the kids he'd be leaving in three weeks.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He was nervous to tell them, so he kind of sidestepped the whole conversation, just said, so you know I might be leaving, right? They were like, yeah, that's what we've been talking about. And then he dropped it. A few days later, Jenni called the girls.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: And then I'm sitting on the couch one day, and my sister's on a call with my mom, and then my mom says something about him leaving in September. And then McKenzie tells me, he's leaving in, like, mid-September. And I was like, what?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: And then she goes and checks her calendar on the phone, and she's like, that's next month.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Yeah, I was like, what the heck, guys? I didn't know this.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I visited the girls in August, weeks before his scheduled departure. McKenzie and Bella were processing this sudden new reality in real time.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I mean, in a year, I had time to get myself kind of ready for it. I was-- like I could spend a little bit more time with my dad. But he's leaving in a month, and there's not really much you can do in a month with your dad.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: And that's literally how, probably, I'm going to think about it, when he's gone, I could have done more.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: It's like he's just going to disappear. Like, he's going to be here one day, and then he's going to be gone.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They were just starting to get their minds around it. For their whole lives, it had been the four of them. Now Fidel would be gone. What would graduation look like? What about wrestling on the weekends, and soccer, which was such a big part of their lives? Fidel was the soccer parent. He'd go to every game.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I realize he's not going to be there for another tournament. (WHIMPERING) So--

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: (WHIMPERING) Yeah. A whole soccer season, he's not going to be here.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Well, he'll be here for the first part of it, barely. I hope he at least gets to come to one more game. Maybe.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: He'll be going to a couple. But yeah.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: I remember, it was the other day, and my mom was still gone, and she was gone. And then my dad was in some place, I don't know, he was outside or something. And I realized, she's going to college next year. My mom's the only one that's going to be here, because my dad's going to be gone. So this is what my life is going to be like for three more years. Like, I'm not going to have anybody to just talk to. So yeah.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: You guys are spreading telepathic messages to one another. What are they?

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: No, I'm not spreading telepathic. I'm just sad, because I didn't even really think about that. OK, I guess I didn't think about how Bella was going to be here all by herself, without people.

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Yeah. Well, I'll have my sports to distract me from things. And I'll probably go to the gym, or something. I have my friends and everything. And I talk to my best friend about-- we'll tell each other everything. But it's just not going to be the same as my sister.

segments.speaker: McKenzie Rivera
segments.text: Yeah, I guess-- that's the same for me. I don't-- well, personally, I don't tell my friends everything. I mostly just tell Bella everything.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The plan was Jenni would stay with the girls. She would work for five more years so she could get her pension, retire. Then she'd join Fidel in Mexico, in the city of Merida, in a nice little neighborhood with lots of expats, far from his family in Mexico. But that's what he wanted. He didn't want to feel like a failure, coming back to the same place all these years later. Jenni and the girls would visit him on school breaks.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: As his departure date approached, the girls started hugging their dad a lot more. Bella even watched one of his favorite TV shows with him, The Voice. Fidel's been acting differently too. He's imparting all the last-minute wisdom he can think of, how to change the car oil, how to fix the stove, how to get the barbecue to work just right.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Make sure you know what is a screwdriver, and you know what is a wrench. But that is this part that got saddening, like angry, because I'm going to leave my kids. I think that is the stuff, when I got angry with myself, like, oh man, I need to leave my kids.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: How do you think your relationship will be, if you're not over here?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: That is going to be a challenge. She's going to be here, I'm going to be there. And some days, they're going to feel alone. And some days I'm going to feel alone. And she's going to be-- I'm pretty sure some days, she's going to be really frustrated, because she got two teenagers. And I'm going to be over there by myself like, no, pretty much no responsibilities. You know? And she's going to have all the work.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: He sucks talking on the phone.

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jenni Rivera
segments.text: He does. I love my husband, he has a lot of great qualities. But on the phone, he's like, uh-huh, mm-hmm, yeah, OK. It is 100%, 100% going to suck for the next five years. There's no question about it. I wake up in the morning, and I have my coffee while I talk to my husband. And I talk to him before I go to bed at night. And I'm like, I don't know how I'm going to manage without him. I really don't.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Can you imagine your life there?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I see my house, big house, empty. I think my only way to spend my time is working, work the most I can, 12 hours, 13 hours, 14 hours.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Why? So you don't have to be alone in the house? Or why?

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Yeah. I don't need to be alone. And I don't need to be depressed, or thinking, and something else. Just stay busy, working.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Since Trump took office, 1.6 million people have self-deported, at least according to the Trump administration. That $1,000 that they offer anyone who self-deports, Fidel refused it. He found it insulting. He didn't want his name part of any official list being used to prove Trump's success. Instead, he decided his own terms of departure, when and how.

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: I can leave for the front door, not the back door. I can live on my own terms. I leave happy, I leave my family happy.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He had planned to take off quietly, but Jenni and the girls refused to let him disappear without a trace, as if he hadn't been here all this time. So they threw a Farewell Fidel party, invited all his friends, his co-workers, and their neighbors to celebrate the last three decades.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: On the day of the party, he disappeared for a while. When he showed back up, he had a massive pinata of Donald Trump, custom-made. They hung it in the backyard. Fidel swung at it, laughing.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: [BANGING]

segments.speaker: Fidel Rivera
segments.text: Ooh!

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And Bella finished it off.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: [BANGING]

segments.speaker: Bella Rivera
segments.text: Oh! What the heck?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Fidel left in October. He pushed back his departure date so he could be there for his 17th wedding anniversary, and for the first soccer tournament of the season.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Valerie Kipnis is a producer on our show. A week after Fidel left, Jenni heard from the school that a father of two kids there was picked up by ICE and is in detention now.
